659.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“to perish”); further discussion of the morphology follows below.

632.t: From γράμμα (grámma, “writing”) + -εύς (-eús, masculine suffix of person concerned).

663.t: Uncertain, but possibly from σιμός (sīmós). As a name for Jews and Christians, used for Biblical Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (šimʿōn).

667.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hréwō, from Proto-Indo-European *sréweti, from *srew- (“to flow; to stream”). Cognates include Sanskrit स्रव॑ति (srávati), Old Church Slavonic строуꙗ (struja, “stream”).

642.t: From Proto-Hellenic *makrós, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós, from *meh₂ḱ- (“to increase”). By surface analysis, μῆκος (mêkos) + -ρός (-rós).

683.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *hwédios, from Proto-Indo-European *swéd-yo-s, from *swé (“self”). Equivalent to ἕ (hé) + -ιος (-ĭos).

698.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰəřřō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer-. The iota in the progressive forms (present system) is a reflex of the *y marker for the present tense added onto the root χαρ- (khar-).

640.t: From ὅδε (hóde). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀃 (o /⁠hō⁠/)

686.t: From Proto-Hellenic *aíks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”). Cognates include Old Armenian այծ (ayc), Sanskrit एड (eḍa), and Albanian dhi.

664.t: From Proto-Hellenic *poimḗn, from Proto-Indo-European *poh₂imḗn, an abstract agent noun formed from an ablaut of *peh₂- (“to protect”) + *-mḗn.

650.t: From Proto-Indo-European *tr̥-ped-ih₂- (“having three feet”), from *tr̥- (“three”, combining form) + *pṓds (“foot”) + *-ih₂ (feminine nominal suffix).

629.t: Earlier Proto-Hellenic *kréwas, from Proto-Indo-European *kréwh₂s. Cognates include Sanskrit क्रविस् (kravís), Latin cruor (Italian crudo), Proto-Slavic *kry, and Old English hrǣw (English raw).

681.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ménō, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay, stand still”). Cognates include Latin maneō (“remain”), Persian ماندن (mândan, “to remain”).

625.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hebdmākontə, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥-ḱómt-h₂, from *septḿ̥(d)ḱomt. Cognates include Sanskrit सप्तति (saptati), Latin septuāgintā and Old Armenian եօթանասուն (eōtʻanasun).

670.t: Perhaps from Proto-Hellenic *eukʰomai (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀄𐀐𐀵 (e-u-ke-to, “εὔχεται (eúkhetai)”)), thematized from Proto-Indo-European *h₁é-h₁ugʰ-tor, reduplicated present from *h₁wegʷʰ- (“to promise, to praise”).

680.t: From Proto-Hellenic *lə́kwos, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus. Cognates include Latin lacus, Old Irish loch, and Old English lagu (English lay).

671.t: From Proto-Hellenic *káwyō, likely from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂w- (“to burn”), with cognates such as Lithuanian kūlė̃ (“smut fungus ("burnt fungus")”), Latvian kūla (“old; dry; grass of last year”), and possibly Persian سو (su, “light”).

666.t: From ἀντί (antĭ́, “in return for”) + ἀποδίδωμι (ăpodĭ́dōmi, “to give back”).

648.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mā́kos, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂ḱos. Cognates include Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬯𐬀𐬵 (masah), Latin maciēs, and Hittite [script needed] (mak-l-ant-).

636.t: From ἀπο- (apo-, “off”) + ὁρίζω (horĭ́zō, “separate”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix).

646.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ō. Cognate with Latin ō̆.

620.t: Uncertain. The etymology determination is complicated by the fact that the word is similar to Ancient Greek κρύπτω (krŭ́ptō, “to hide; cover”) in form and sense, thus indicating possible (bi-directional) analogical influence.

689.t: From δια- (dĭă-, “apart”) + ψάλμα (psắlmă, “psalm”); hence literally “apart from the psalm”.

655.t: Frozen adverbial accusative of *πάλις (*pális) from Proto-Indo-European *kʷl̥His, from *kʷel- (“to revolve”) (whence πέλω (pélō, “to go, be”) and πάλαι (pálai, “before, long ago”)).

617.t: From an unattested *αἶτος (*aîtos, “something given: allotment, share”) + -έω (-éō, denominal verb suffix), the former from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ey- (“to give, take”), whence also αἴνυμαι (aínumai), αἶσα (aîsa), αἴτιος (aítios), διαιτάω (diaitáō).

665.t: Of uncertain origin, though probably of Indo-European origin.

679.t: Uncertain. In earlier literature, the term was derived from Proto-Indo-European *ḱōymeh₂, itself related to Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos.

631.t: From ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + ἵστημι (hĭ́stēmĭ, “to stand”). Compare ἐπίσταμαι (epĭ́stămai).

633.t: From εὔχομαι (eúkhomai, “to pray; to wish”) + -η (-ē, noun-forming suffix).

685.t: Ultimately from αἶσχος (aîskhos, “disgrace”). According to Beekes, a back-formation from αἰσχύνω (aiskhúnō, “to disgrace”).

687.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dwān, from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂-m, from the root *dweh₂- (“long, far”). Related to δηρός (dērós).

622.t: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek; compare σῆραγξ (sêrănx) and φάλαγξ (phắlănx). Furnée compares also μάραγοι (máragoi, “overhanging places”) and Spanish barranca (“ravine”).

601.t: Unknown. It has been proposed to be a blend between θλάω (thláō, “to crush, bruise”) and φλίβω (phlíbō, “to squeeze”).

635.t: Of unknown origin, with no known cognates outside Greek. Furnée connects φάσγανον (phásganon, “sword”) as φασγ-/σφαγ-, suggesting a Pre-Greek origin.

653.t: The neuter inflected form of ἐνύπνιος (enúpnios).

610.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydt (“to split”). Cognate with Sanskrit भेदति (bhedati, “to split”) and Gothic 𐌱𐌴𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (beitan, “to bite”).

634.t: From the root of προσήλυθον (prosḗluthon, aorist of προσέρχομαι (prosérkhomai, “to approach”)) + -τος (-tos), thus literally, “one that has approached”.
